transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2028-07-12 14:00 UTC
Duration: 53 minutes
Attendees: Alex Mercer (Redwood AE), Priya Shah (Redwood SE), Michael Tan (CTO - Stellaris), Lisa Kwan (Eng Mgr), Jonah Perez (SRE)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be noisy):
Stellaris is evaluating Redwood for a mixed hosted/dedicated deployment. Key concerns: regional failover, cost of reserved capacity vs burst, private VPC fit, KMS and audit logs, traffic steering during incidents. They want a pilot to validate SLA and cold start behavior.

Topics:
- Fallback composition (hot-standby, regional steering, traffic split)
- Dedicated capacity sizing + burst behavior
- Private/VPC constraints and data residency
- SLA expectations and incident mitigation playbook
- Benchmarking plan and next steps

Transcript body:
[00:00] Alex Mercer: Hey everyone thanks for joining, I'm Alex from Redwood, this is Priya our solutions engineer, um we'll run through how we approach multi region fallback and what dedicated looks like, and collect your constraints.
[00:18] Michael Tan: Hey Alex, yeah thanks, trying to keep this short — we have a hard deadline to pick a vendor by end of month, security is heavy on this.
[00:25] Lisa Kwan: Hi all, quick context: we run inference for routing decisions in our edge stacks, p95 needs to be under 120ms for customer facing endpoints, we also have a batch of async jobs that can tolerate higher latency.
[00:40] Priya Shah: Got it. When you say edge stacks — is that a per-region routing, or centralized?
[00:47] Jonah Perez: It's regional — most traffic originates in NA and EU, Asia is smaller but grows fast. We need region steering and ability to fail traffic to another region if a zone goes down.
[00:58] Alex Mercer: Okay, we support policy-based routing by region and can do automatic fallback to compatible model variants. Important note: hosted mode lets you use Redwood's global infra, dedicated gives reserved GPU pools in a region, and private is VPC/on-prem.
[01:14] Michael Tan: Two immediate questions — how graceful is degradation? Do you have automatic canary to fall back, and what counts toward our SLA if region A is down?
[01:25] Priya Shah: Yeah so we have multi-tier fallbacks: 1) local prefix cache and KV reuse to reduce token generation; 2) route to warm hot-standby in same region (if reserved capacity), 3) route to another region's compatible model variant, 4) degrade to lower-cost quantized variant or queued async.
[01:43] Lisa Kwan: When you say warm hot-standby — what's the warm duration? if idle for long do we pay to keep models hot?
[01:49] Priya Shah: Warm time depends on reserved pools and your burst config. For Dedicated you can keep a minimum pool and autoscale. If you use hosted we do transient instances and there is a small cold-start window — typically 4–12 seconds for large models, but for our inference engine we've reduced that with pre-warm heuristics.
[02:07] Jonah Perez: 4–12 seconds is kinda long for our sync path — that will blow p95. Can you route to a smaller low-latency model automatically while the larger one spins up?
[02:18] Priya Shah: Yes, traffic split rules can route to a faster quantized variant and then backfill results when the main finishes, or you can do a hedged request to both and take first response. Hedging increases cost.
[02:30] Michael Tan: Cost is major — our CFO will push back on always-on dedicated capacity. What's the economics of a small reserved pool plus burst?
[02:38] Alex Mercer: Common pattern: reserve a baseline to meet your typical p50/p90 traffic, configure burst autoscale for spiky periods. Redwood Optimize gives suggestions for batch sizes and quantization to hit cost targets. We'll include sample numbers in the pricing worksheet.
[02:50] Lisa Kwan: Security — SSO/SAML, audit logs, and KMS; we need customer-controlled keys and evidence of audit log retention for 12 months.
[02:58] Priya Shah: Private deployments support customer KMS/HSM and full audit log streaming to your SIEM. Hosted supports KMS with BYOK options and audit log exports. We'll share our SOC2 pack and the sample audit log schema.
[03:12] Michael Tan: Great. What about failover routing? We don't want region B to get overloaded when A goes down and cause cascading failures.
[03:21] Priya Shah: You can define capacity-aware routing rules: weight by available tokens or capacity units and gradually shift traffic based on health signals. We also have circuit-breaker thresholds to stop sending traffic to a degraded region.
[03:33] Jonah Perez: Who controls those signals? Our control plane or Redwood? We want the ability to flip to manual quickly.
[03:40] Alex Mercer: You get control plane hooks and can set automatic or manual policies. There's a routing API and UI in Redwood Console for on-call teams to flip policies; we usually recommend automated with manual override.
[03:54] Lisa Kwan: Does Redwood expose tracing for token-level latency? We need token-level breakdown for troubleshooting.
[03:59] Priya Shah: Yes, Console gives per-token latency histograms and token-cost breakdown, can be sampled and connected to distributed tracing.
[04:08] Michael Tan: Okay, let's dig into an outage scenario: US-East loses a rack; how does traffic move and what is considered downtime for our SLA?
[04:18] Priya Shah: Typically you define SLOs per-route. If US-East is fully down we can fail to US-West or EU, SLA can be region-specific. For Hosted, our SLA covers availability across configured regions depending on plan; Dedicated contracts can have stricter regional SLAs. We'll map that to your routes when scoping.
[04:36] Jonah Perez: Does the SLA cover model output quality regressions after failover? If we switch to quantized variant, results might differ.
[04:45] Alex Mercer: SLA is availability and latency; quality is handled via canary and evals. We recommend golden prompt sets and automated regression alerts tied to rollouts so you can detect quality drift.
[04:58] Michael Tan: Are rollbacks instant? If a variant shows drift, can we automatically revert?
[05:03] Priya Shah: Yes, rollouts support automatic rollback based on quality and latency thresholds. You can also configure traffic caps during rollout.
[05:12] Lisa Kwan: On private fit: our legal team wants data never leave our VPC — can Redwood do an air-gapped on-prem deploy?
[05:20] Alex Mercer: We offer an on-prem package for regulated workloads. It includes private control plane and local inference nodes. There's more ops overhead but it meets that constraint.
[05:29] Michael Tan: Ops overhead acceptable if it passes security. How do we test it — we prefer a pilot that simulates a region outage and measures failover time and error rates.
[05:38] Priya Shah: Totally doable. We can run a synthetic qps benchmark, simulate region failure by toggling route health, and capture latency and error rates. We'll provide a benchmark plan and scripts.
[05:48] Jonah Perez: Also need to stress cold starts — measure cost delta for hedging vs keeping N instances hot.
[05:55] Priya Shah: We'll include hedging cost models in the worksheet.
[06:00] Michael Tan: Who from Redwood would lead the pilot?
[06:04] Alex Mercer: Priya will own the technical run and I'll coordinate procurement/contract.
[06:09] Lisa Kwan: Good. A few small things — do you support region-specific model pinning? We need EU traffic to always use EU-hosted model for residency.
[06:18] Priya Shah: Yes, route pinning by model version and region is supported. You can also set fallbacks that honor data residency rules so EU traffic only fails within EU variants or to an approved fallback.
[06:29] Michael Tan: And audit trail for who changed routing rules?
[06:33] Alex Mercer: RBAC plus audit logs, changes are recorded with user id and timestamp.
[06:38] Jonah Perez: Latency targets again — if we accept a slight p95 slip during failover, what does that look like?
[06:45] Priya Shah: During cross-region failover you'll see added network RTT; typical p95 delta depends on region distance — for NA->EU it's ~80–150ms extra, but you can mitigate with local smaller model and async backfill pattern.
[07:00] Michael Tan: That matches our rough numbers. Next, procurement — what are minimum terms for Dedicated?
[07:07] Alex Mercer: Dedicated is typically monthly reserved pools with commit tiers; we can do a short pilot commitment as a bridge. We'll outline options in the pricing doc.
[07:16] Lisa Kwan: Any gotchas with KV cache persistence during failover? If cache doesn't move, we might lose context and increase token cost.
[07:25] Priya Shah: KV cache is local to the serving instance. We have prefix cache strategies and cross-region warmers that proactively populate caches in standby regions for high-value prefixes. It's an optional cost but effective.
[07:40] Jonah Perez: Sounds like we should pilot with a subset of prefixes to measure hit rate.
[07:44] Priya Shah: Exactly, and Redwood Optimize can recommend which prompts to prime.
[07:50] Michael Tan: Are there any limits on routing API rate or how fast we can flip traffic?
[07:55] Alex Mercer: Routing API is low-latency and meant for on-call automation, flips are immediate; we recommend coupling with circuit-breaker and gradual weights when possible.
[08:05] Lisa Kwan: About canary windows — how long do you usually run canaries before full rollout?
[08:11] Priya Shah: Depends on traffic volume; often 5–10% for 30–60 minutes to get meaningful signal, but you can set auto thresholds to scale it.
[08:22] Michael Tan: Ok seems fine. Any mention of competitor approaches that matter?
[08:26] Alex Mercer: Some competitors require you to build your own traffic steering — Redwood provides it as config with tracing and audit logs; note sometimes open platforms give more control but more ops lift.
[08:37] Jonah Perez: We heard VastAI had cheaper burst but no model-level routing — noted.
[08:43] Lisa Kwan: For the pilot, we want success criteria: failover < 10s to a compatible path for 95% of requests OR p95 under 250ms within 30s of failover, and no more than 2x cost increase during incident.
[08:58] Priya Shah: That's specific and doable to test. We'll put it into the pilot plan.
[09:04] Michael Tan: Also include quality regression thresholds — automatic rollback if eval score drops >5% on golden prompts.
[09:12] Alex Mercer: Noted.
[09:15] Lisa Kwan: Procurement — we need sample contract language about data residency and an SLA appendix.
[09:21] Alex Mercer: We'll provide sample SLA appendix and enterprise addendum.
[09:25] Michael Tan: Great. A few quick clarifications from Jonah — what metrics will we see in Console during the failover in real time?
[09:32] Jonah Perez: (speaking up) sorry, question — will we get active capacity utilization per pool?
[09:36] Priya Shah: Yes, Console shows capacity units, queued requests, per-model utilization, and health signals. You can hook alerts to any metric.
[09:44] Jonah Perez: Perfect.
[09:46] Lisa Kwan: I'm a little worried about the cold-start numbers you mentioned earlier if we go hosted. Do you have a published benchmark for model sizes and cold-start latency?
[09:55] Alex Mercer: We have perf profiles per model in the catalog; they'll show typical cold-start and per-token latencies on x86 and GPU flavors. We'll attach a link in the follow-up.
[10:05] Michael Tan: Okay, let's try to sketch the pilot scope now — time boxed to two weeks, include: synthetic load test, simulated region failure, cold-start hedging cost analysis, and audit log validation.
[10:15] Priya Shah: Sounds good, and we'll include a small canary in production with limited traffic as part of week two if you want.
[10:22] Michael Tan: Yes please. Also we want one run in private (VPC) and one in hosted to compare.
[10:28] Alex Mercer: We can do that — private pilot will require a bit more setup. We'll provide a checklist.
[10:33] Lisa Kwan: Regarding the private pilot, what is the earliest timeline?
[10:36] Priya Shah: If your infra team is ready, we can stand up a private control plane in about 7–10 business days for a basic POC.
[10:44] Jonah Perez: Any special networking requirements?
[10:47] Priya Shah: We'll need peering/VPN and firewall rules; we'll share a network guide.
[10:52] Michael Tan: Ok. I think that's the bulk. Any other risks we should discuss?
[10:57] Alex Mercer: The usual: model compatibility across quantized variants, cross-region latency, and cost during sustained failover. We'll build a risk register in the pilot plan.
[11:06] Lisa Kwan: Fine. Shall we summarize next steps?
[11:09] Alex Mercer: Sure. Priya will draft the pilot plan and failover topology, I'll send pricing and SLA appendix, Michael will share traffic profiles and golden prompts, and Jonah will validate network readiness.
[11:20] Michael Tan: Good. Can we get those docs by Monday?
[11:23] Alex Mercer: We'll target Monday 2028-07-15.
[11:27] Lisa Kwan: Thanks all.
[11:30] Jonah Perez: Thanks.
[11:32] Alex Mercer: Thanks everyone, we'll follow-up in email with links to SOC2 pack and the pricing spreadsheet.
[11:40] Michael Tan: Bye.
